title: Bond reconstruction and vacancy clustering in monolayer silicon carbide from first principles
abstract: Bond reconstruction in vacancy-related structures affects their formation energies, symmetries, and electronic and optical properties. Using density functional theory, we investigate bond reconstruction mechanisms of monovacancies and vacancy aggregates in monolayer silicon carbide. Multiple bond descriptors reveal that isolated monovacancies undergo both in-plane reconstruction and out-of-plane distortion, which together shape their stability and electronic structure. For compact vacancy aggregates, we show that bond reconstruction acts as a key stabilization mechanism. However, in carbon monovacancy, reconstruction suppresses optical activity. In contrast, a highly stable aggregate composed of three carbon vacancies surrounding a silicon vacancy emerges as a promising infrared color-center candidate, combining a triplet ground state with a favorable Debye-Waller factor of the emission. These results highlight the role of bond reconstruction in defining the quantum properties of vacancy defects in two-dimensional silicon carbide.
summary: The research uses first-principles DFT to study how bond reconstruction stabilizes vacancy defects in 2D SiC. It identifies a specific vacancy cluster as an excellent candidate for quantum color centers, characterized by a stable triplet spin state and predictable near-infrared optical emission signatures.
main_problem: The study investigates how bond reconstruction mechanisms affect the formation energies, symmetries, and quantum properties of intrinsic defects (monovacancies and aggregates) in monolayer silicon carbide.
main_result: A specific vacancy aggregate ($	ext{VSi}_3	ext{VC}$) was identified as a promising infrared color-center candidate due to its stable triplet ground state and favorable emission characteristics.
method: Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations, utilizing advanced techniques like $	ext{HSE06}$ hybrid functionals, $	ext{cNEB}$ for relaxation paths, and analysis of hyperfine coupling parameters were employed.
model_or_system: The physical system is monolayer silicon carbide ($	ext{SiC}$) containing various point defects, including single vacancies ($	ext{V}_{	ext{Si}}$, $	ext{V}_{	ext{C}}$) and larger vacancy clusters. The calculations model the structural relaxation and electronic state changes upon defect formation.
key_observables: Spin ground state ($S=1$ triplet), Zero-Field Splitting ($	ext{ZFS}$) parameter $D$, hyperfine coupling tensors, localized vibration modes ($	ext{LVMs}$), and optical transition energies (near-infrared range).
important_parameters: Formation energy ($E_f$), Debye-Waller factor, Huang-Rhys factor ($	ext{HR} \approx 0.59$), and the electronic structure derived from $	ext{HSE06}$ calculations.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that bond reconstruction dictates the final stable quantum state of the defect; approximations are made regarding the calculation of excited states and finite-size corrections for energy levels.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate out-of-plane displacement patterns, reaction paths showing chirality swapping barriers, ground state Kohn-Sham level structures, and phonon sideband simulations detailing localized vibration modes ($	ext{LVMs}$).
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes isolated monovacancies first, demonstrating symmetry breaking upon reconstruction. It then moves to vacancy aggregates, culminating in the detailed quantum characterization of the $	ext{VSi}_3	ext{VC}$ cluster's optical and spin properties.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses defect engineering for solid-state quantum emitters by calculating measurable spectroscopic fingerprints ($	ext{ZFS}$, $	ext{LVMs}$) based on fundamental structural changes (bond reconstruction).

Bond reconstruction and out-of-plane distortion in monovacancy defects in monolayer SiC. a) Electron localization function (ELF) at 0.7 isovalue level (yellow) in the VSi and VC defects, comparing dangling and reconstructed bond calculations. The presence of nodal planes and the localization and direction of the lobes differentiate the two cases. Silicon and carbon atoms are illustrated as blue and brown balls, respectively. b) Accompanying out-of-plane distortion after bond reconstruction in VSi and VC defects, respectively. The displacement field is visualized as a heatmap projected onto the monolayer. Atomic sites of silicon and carbon are illustrated as larger and smaller...

FIG. 2. Reorientation of the chirality in the VC defect calculated using the climbing image NEB method at the PBE functional level. a) Chirality swap reaction path through an in-plane barrier geometry. b) Chirality swap and rotation through an out-of-plane barrier geometry. Insets show the out-of-plane distortion heatmap projected on the SiC monolayer plane in the corresponding structures along the reaction path.

FIG. 3. Ground state Kohn-Sham level structures in spin-polarized HSE06 calculations in a) the VC and b) the VSi3VC defects. Defect orbitals inside the bandgap are labelled according to the irreducible representations in a) C2 and b) D3h point groups. Insets show the pseudo-wavefunction of the corresponding defect orbitals. Excited states are described via spin-conserving single-electron promotion to the unoccupied levels.

FIG. 4. Systematic construction of compact vacancy aggre- gate models. Atoms with dangling or frustrated bonds are considered as primary vacancy sites in the models as shown in the 3VC →VSi3VC and VC →VSiVC constructions, respec- tively. For the compact clusters that involve antisite defects, elements are swapped at the edge of the cluster or at recon- structed bonding sites, as illustrated in the VSi2VC →3VC and VSiVC →2VC construction, respectively.

FIG. 5. Calculated structures of compact vacancy aggregates. a) and b) show the evolution of the formation and binding energies at the PBE level, respectively. Interpolated lines connect the calculation points to guide the eye. c) Geometry and ELF plots of the VSi + nVC series. The ground state point symmetry and spin are labelled for these structures.
